answerSpec.modelAnswer: Relations worsened partly because the two powers had opposed systems: once Hitler was defeated, the USA and the USSR had little left in common, and each saw the other's ideology as a threat. The most immediate dispute was Eastern Europe. Stalin wanted a buffer zone of friendly governments and imposed a pro-communist government in Poland, which the West saw as breaking the Yalta promise of free elections. Attitudes then hardened. Truman, President from April 1945, was more suspicious than Roosevelt, and the American atomic bomb alarmed Stalin. In 1946 Kennan's Long Telegram and Churchill's Iron Curtain speech showed that Western leaders now saw the USSR as an enemy, while Stalin called Churchill a warmonger.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Potsdam showed how far relations had fallen. The leaders argued over reparations, over the government of Poland and over Soviet influence in Eastern Europe, and accepted the new Polish border only for the time being. The atmosphere had changed: Truman was more suspicious than Roosevelt, Attlee replaced Churchill midway, and Truman's mention of a powerful new weapon showed that the USA now had the atomic bomb.

However, Potsdam reflected the breakdown more than it caused it. The USA and the USSR had been ideological enemies since 1917, and the West remembered the Nazi-Soviet Pact. The dispute over Poland had begun before Yalta and continued after it, since Stalin's idea of 'free elections' meant governments friendly to the USSR. After Potsdam, the bomb, the Long Telegram and the Iron Curtain speech hardened attitudes further.

I disagree with the statement. Potsdam revealed the disagreements, but the main reason for the breakdown was the clash of ideologies and security needs, shown in the struggle over Eastern Europe, which no conference could settle.

stem: This question is about the origins of the Cold War.

parts.stem: Describe the Berlin airlift.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: When the USSR blockaded West Berlin in June 1948, the Americans and British supplied the city by air through three air corridors. They flew in food, fuel and especially coal; at the height of the airlift a plane landed every few minutes, and historians estimate about 2.3 million tonnes were delivered. The airlift continued until Stalin lifted the blockade in May 1949.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The USA introduced Marshall Aid mainly to contain communism. Truman's government believed that poverty and hunger after the war made people turn to communism, so rebuilding Europe's economies would make communism less attractive. This fear was sharpened by events: the Greek civil war, strong communist parties in France and Italy, and, in February 1948, the communist takeover in Czechoslovakia, which persuaded Congress to approve the aid. There were also economic reasons: a prosperous Europe would buy American goods, which helped American industry and avoided a post-war slump.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There is a strong case against the USSR. Stalin broke the Yalta promise of free elections: communists gained control of Eastern Europe through salami tactics and rigged elections, as in Poland in 1947, and the Czech coup of 1948 destroyed the last democracy in the region. In 1948 the USSR blockaded West Berlin, trying to force the West out by cutting off supplies to two million civilians. Traditional historians therefore blame the USSR.

Revisionist historians point to American actions. The USA used its atomic monopoly to put pressure on the USSR, and the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid extended American influence into Europe, which Stalin called dollar imperialism. In Germany the West merged its zones and introduced the Deutschmark without Soviet agreement, which provoked the blockade.

I largely agree. Both sides acted from fear, as post-revisionists argue, but the Soviet imposition of communist governments on Eastern Europe came first and caused most of the American reactions, so the USSR bears more of the blame, though not all of it.

The USSR was boycotting the Council over China's seat, so it could not use its veto, and the Council called on member states to help South Korea. A UN force was formed under General MacArthur; most troops were American, but others came from countries such as Britain, Turkey and Canada.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: China entered the war because the UN went beyond defending South Korea. After Inchon, UN forces crossed the 38th parallel in October 1950, captured Pyongyang and advanced towards the Yalu River, China's border. The new communist government, set up only in 1949, feared that an American-led army on its border might attack China itself. China warned that it would intervene, but MacArthur did not take the warning seriously. It also wished to keep a friendly communist state as a buffer between itself and the Americans.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
MacArthur bears much responsibility. After Inchon he pressed forward to the Yalu River, dismissing China's warnings and spreading his forces thinly, so the Chinese attacks of late 1950 drove the UN back south of the 38th parallel. His public calls to attack China then caused a crisis with Truman, who dismissed him in April 1951.

However, he was not acting alone. Truman and the UN approved the advance into North Korea, so the change from containment to rollback was a political decision. The decisive factor was China's intervention with huge forces. After that, Truman chose a limited war, refusing to attack China or use atomic weapons, because he feared war with China and the USSR; this meant Korea could not be united by force.

I only partly agree. MacArthur's misjudgement made the defeat of 1950 worse, but Korea stayed divided because China would not accept a hostile Korea on its border and the USA would not risk a wider war to change that.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The USA became involved because of containment and the domino theory: Eisenhower warned in 1954 that if Vietnam fell, its neighbours would follow. After the French defeat, the Geneva Agreements divided Vietnam, and the USA backed Ngo Dinh Diem's South Vietnam with money, weapons and advisers, supporting his refusal to hold the 1956 elections that Ho Chi Minh was expected to win. When the National Liberation Front began a guerrilla war in 1960, Kennedy increased the number of American advisers to about 16,000, because abandoning an ally would damage American credibility against the USSR and China.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Tet was a turning point in American opinion. In January 1968 the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese attacked more than a hundred towns and cities and entered the US embassy compound in Saigon. Americans had been told the war was being won, so Tet destroyed public trust. In March Johnson announced he would not seek re-election, and American policy moved towards negotiation and withdrawal.

However, militarily Tet was a communist defeat: the attackers suffered very heavy losses and the Viet Cong were badly weakened. Other turning points also matter. The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution of 1964 and the arrival of combat troops in 1965 turned an advisory role into a full war, while Nixon's Vietnamisation from 1969 began the actual withdrawal, completed after the Paris Peace Accords of 1973.

I largely agree. Tet did not change the military balance, but it changed what Americans were willing to accept, and every later step towards withdrawal followed from that loss of support.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Hungarians resented the harsh Stalinist rule of Rákosi, whose secret police imprisoned thousands. Living standards were low, and many blamed the USSR for taking Hungarian resources on unfair terms; Catholics resented persecution of the Church, and nationalists resented Soviet troops on Hungarian soil. answerSpec.modelAnswer:
In one sense the crises show that control was secure. Both times the USSR restored control within days or weeks, installed loyal leaders, Kádár and later Husák, and suffered no Western response, since the USA would not risk war in the Soviet sphere. The Brezhnev Doctrine warned other satellites not to try.

But the crises also show insecurity. In both countries communist parties themselves had moved towards reform, and the people supported them; control could be restored only with tanks. Opposition kept returning: in East Germany in 1953, in the flight to the West that forced the Berlin Wall in 1961, and in Poland with Solidarity in 1980. When Gorbachev refused to use force in 1989, Soviet control collapsed within months.

I disagree with the statement. The crises show that Soviet control was secure only as long as the USSR was willing to use force; it rested on military power, not on the consent of the people.

In December 1981 Jaruzelski declared martial law, banned Solidarity and detained its leaders.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The Wall was built to stop East Germans escaping to the West. Berlin was the one open border, and roughly 2.5 to 3 million people left between 1949 and 1961, with numbers rising sharply in 1961. Many were young and skilled, so the brain drain damaged the East German economy and was a huge embarrassment to a state that claimed communism was better. Khrushchev had tried to force the Western powers out of Berlin in 1958 and again at Vienna in 1961, but they refused, so closing the border in August 1961 solved the problem without fighting the West.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Gorbachev's role was crucial. Unlike his predecessors in 1956 and 1968, he made clear that the USSR would not use force to keep communist governments in power, and in 1989 he accepted Solidarity's election victory and kept Soviet troops in their barracks in East Germany. His policies of glasnost and perestroika also encouraged people in the satellites to demand change.

However, he did not create the crisis. The Soviet and Eastern European economies had been stagnating for years, the satellites were in debt, and the arms race and the war in Afghanistan drained resources; these problems were why he needed reform. The collapse was also driven from below: Solidarity had survived martial law, and in 1989 crowds in Leipzig, Berlin and Prague forced their governments out.

Some women's lives changed a great deal. answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The New Deal had real successes. The bank holiday, the Emergency Banking Act and the fireside chats saved the banking system in 1933 and restored confidence. Agencies such as the CCC, FERA and WPA gave work or relief to millions, and the TVA, Social Security and the Wagner Act brought lasting changes. Democracy survived at a time when the Depression helped extremists elsewhere.

But it did not end the Depression. The New Deal was successful in relief and reform but only partly in recovery, the problem that mattered most to the unemployed.

**Background information.** In March 1946 Winston Churchill, no longer Prime Minister, spoke at Fulton, Missouri, with President Truman in the audience, warning that an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe. Stalin denounced the speech. Over the next two years communists took control across Eastern Europe, and the USA answered with the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Aid. Historians still debate which side was more to blame.

Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a cartoon of the kind published in a British newspaper in March 1946, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> A huge bearded figure in a military greatcoat, with a pipe, peers over a high wall that runs across a map of Europe. Behind the wall, small figures labelled with the names of Eastern European countries sit in a fenced yard. A sign on the wall reads "No admittance by order".

**Source B** — a commentary of the kind broadcast on Soviet radio in March 1946 (invented for this question)

> Mr Churchill and his friends want the English-speaking nations to rule the world. They forget that the Soviet people lost more than any other in defeating Hitler, and that the countries on our border have twice been the road for armies marching into Russia. We ask only that these neighbours be friendly. Is that a curtain, or a fence around a house that has been burned twice?

**Source C** — a report written by a fictional American diplomat in Warsaw for the State Department, January 1947 (invented for this question)

> The election was not free. Opposition candidates were struck off the lists in many districts, thousands of their supporters were arrested before polling day, and security police stood inside the polling stations. The government bloc has announced a large majority. I see no prospect of the promises made at Yalta being honoured.

**Source D** — a letter from a fictional Czech teacher to a cousin in Canada, March 1948 (invented for this question)

> You ask whether the Russians invaded. They did not; there is not one Russian soldier in Prague. Our own communists did it, with crowds in the streets, workers' militias with rifles and a frightened President. Some of my colleagues cheered. Others have already lost their posts. Nobody speaks freely in the staff room now.

**Source E** — a cartoon of the kind published in a Soviet magazine in 1947, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> A plump man in a top hat decorated with stars and stripes offers a basket of bread to a thin European woman. Under the bread, the basket is full of chains, a contract labelled "Bases" and a padlock. In the background stands a factory with an American flag flying over it.

**Source F** — from a speech by a fictional American congressman to his voters in Ohio, 1948 (invented for this question)

> Some say we should mind our own business. But where Stalin's army stands, there is no free press and no free vote, and he will go as far as we let him. Aid to Europe is cheaper than war, and it is the only language the Kremlin respects: strength.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Study Source A. What is the cartoonist's message? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge.

points.description: Message: Stalin / the USSR has cut Eastern Europe off and controls it like a prison
Details: the wall across Europe, fenced yard, 'No admittance'
Context: Iron Curtain speech; Soviet control of Poland and other states

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The cartoonist's message is that Stalin has cut Eastern Europe off from the West and holds its countries like prisoners. The figure in a greatcoat with a pipe, representing Stalin, looks over a wall drawn across Europe, while small figures labelled as Eastern European countries sit in a fenced yard, and the sign 'No admittance by order' shows the West is shut out. This fits the context: in March 1946 Churchill warned that an iron curtain had descended across Europe, and Stalin had already imposed a pro-communist government on Poland. The cartoon supports Churchill's view.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sources agree on the basic fact that the USSR had drawn a line in Europe and controlled the countries on its border: A shows a wall and B admits that the USSR wants these neighbours to be 'friendly'. But they disagree completely about what this means. A presents it as imprisonment, with countries held in a fenced yard behind a wall marked 'No admittance'. B presents it as defence, a 'fence around a house that has been burned twice', because the border countries had been the route for invasions of Russia. B also turns the accusation around, saying Churchill wants the English-speaking nations to rule the world. A British cartoon and Soviet radio were each defending their own side's view, so overall they disagree far more than they agree.

Link to Cominform / 'dollar imperialism'

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The cartoon was published to persuade Soviet and Eastern European readers to reject Marshall Aid. In June 1947 George Marshall offered American aid to rebuild Europe, including the east; Stalin refused it and forced satellites such as Czechoslovakia to refuse too. The cartoon shows why the Soviet government wanted people to distrust the offer: the basket of bread hides chains, a contract for military bases and a padlock, and an American flag flies over a European factory, suggesting that the aid would lead to American control. It reflects the Soviet line that Marshall Aid was 'dollar imperialism', and it appeared as Stalin set up the Cominform to tighten control of the communist parties.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source C is useful because it describes the methods used in Poland in January 1947: opposition candidates were removed, their supporters arrested, and security police stood in the polling stations. It is a private report to the State Department, written immediately by someone who was there, so it is likely to be careful, though an American diplomat had reason to see the worst in communist actions. My own knowledge confirms that the Polish elections were rigged and that the opposition leader Mikołajczyk later fled. Source D is useful because it shows a different method: in Czechoslovakia there were no Soviet troops, and local communists took power with crowds, armed militias and pressure on a frightened President. As a private letter from an eyewitness it has little reason to deceive. Each source covers only one country, but together they are very useful, because they show that control came through local communists using rigged elections, police and pressure as well as through the Red Army.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Several sources support the view that the USSR was to blame. Source A shows Eastern Europe walled off and imprisoned, Source C shows rigged elections in Poland that broke the promise of free elections made at Yalta, and Source D shows communists seizing power in Czechoslovakia with militias and intimidation. Source F argues that Stalin would go as far as he was allowed. C and D are the most convincing: they are private, written close to events, and confirmed by what we know about Poland in 1947 and the Czech coup in 1948. A and F are less convincing because they were written to persuade a public audience.

Other sources suggest the West shared the blame. Source B argues that the USSR wanted only friendly neighbours after being invaded twice, and Source E presents Marshall Aid as a hidden attempt at American control. Both are Soviet propaganda, so they are not reliable as evidence of American motives, but B's point about security is supported by the huge Soviet losses in the war, and the USA did use aid and its atomic monopoly to extend its influence.

Overall the sources provide fairly convincing evidence that Soviet actions in Eastern Europe were the main cause of the breakdown, because the most reliable sources describe Soviet methods directly, but they also show that each side saw its own actions as defensive.

**Background information.** In June 1948 the Western powers introduced a new currency in their zones of Germany. The USSR then cut all land routes to West Berlin. The Western powers supplied the city by air until the blockade was lifted in May 1949. Historians disagree about which side was responsible for the crisis.

Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a statement of the kind issued by the Soviet military administration in Germany, June 1948 (invented for this question)

> The separate currency introduced in the western zones threatens to flood the Soviet zone with worthless old notes and to wreck its economy. The Western powers have abandoned the agreements of Potsdam and are building a separate West German state. Temporary measures on the transport routes are necessary to protect the population of the Soviet zone.

**Source B** — an editorial in a fictional London newspaper, July 1948 (invented for this question)

> Stalin has decided to starve two million Berliners into submission. He calls it 'technical difficulties' on the railway. Nobody is fooled. If we leave Berlin, no European will trust a Western promise again.

**Source C** — the diary of a fictional West Berlin housewife, January 1949 (invented for this question)

> Two hours of electricity tonight, from two until four in the morning, so I got up to iron. Potatoes are dried and taste of cardboard. But every few minutes the planes come in over the roofs. My neighbour, who lost her husband to an American bomb in 1944, waves at them now.

**Source D** — a cartoon of the kind published in East German newspapers in 1948, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> An American general rides on a bomber labelled "Airlift". Instead of food, the bomber drops leaflets marked "Propaganda" and coins marked "Deutschmark" onto a city. In the corner, a worker labelled "Berlin" sweeps the coins away with a broom.

**Source E** — a letter from a fictional American pilot on the airlift to his parents, 1949 (invented for this question)

> Last year I was bombing this country; now I fly flour and coal into it three times a day. The kids at the end of the runway wave handkerchiefs. I don't know much about politics, but I know you don't make a city hungry because you don't like its money.

**Source F** — an article by a fictional historian in a history magazine, 1998 (invented for this question)

> The Western currency reform was a deliberate step towards a West German state, taken without Soviet agreement, and Stalin had genuine reasons to fear it. But his chosen response, to cut off a civilian population, handed the West a moral victory, a military alliance and a divided Germany: the very outcome he most wanted to avoid.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source C shows that life in West Berlin was hard: electricity was available only for two hours in the middle of the night, so the writer got up to iron, and the food was dried potatoes that tasted of cardboard. It also shows that the airlift was constant, with planes coming in every few minutes. Most strikingly, attitudes had changed: a neighbour whose husband was killed by an American bomb in 1944 now waved at the planes. I can infer that the blockade had failed to break morale and had turned West Berliners towards the Western allies.

Source A blames the West: the new currency threatened to wreck the Soviet zone's economy, and the Western powers had abandoned Potsdam and were building a separate West German state, so the 'temporary measures' were defensive. Source B blames Stalin, saying he intended to starve two million Berliners into submission and that his excuses about 'technical difficulties' fooled nobody. answerSpec.modelAnswer: The cartoon was published because the airlift was becoming a propaganda disaster for the USSR: Western planes were keeping West Berlin alive, and the city's people were turning towards the West. The East German press wanted to change how the airlift was seen. The cartoon shows the airlift as a military and political operation, a bomber dropping propaganda and Deutschmarks rather than food, and a worker labelled 'Berlin' sweeping the coins away. Its purpose was to persuade East Germans and Berliners that the airlift was not humanitarian, that the new currency was an American trick, and that ordinary Berliners rejected it.

Some sources support the view that the Western powers were responsible. Source A says the new currency threatened the Soviet zone and that the West had abandoned Potsdam, and Source D presents the airlift as a currency and propaganda operation. Source F, the most balanced source, agrees that the currency reform was a deliberate step towards a West German state taken without Soviet agreement. **Background information.** In 1989 communist rule collapsed across Eastern Europe: Solidarity won the Polish elections in June, Hungary opened its border, the Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November, and the communists fell in Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Romania. Mikhail Gorbachev, Soviet leader since 1985, did not use force to stop these changes. Historians debate how far he was responsible.

Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a cartoon of the kind published in Western newspapers in late 1989, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> A Soviet leader with a birthmark on his forehead stands at an open gate in a long wall. He holds a large key and bows politely as crowds of people, carrying the flags of Poland, Hungary, East Germany and Czechoslovakia, stream out past him.

**Source B** — the memoir of a fictional Solidarity organiser from Gdańsk, published in 2004 (invented for this question)

> People abroad think freedom was a gift from Moscow. It was not. We struck in 1980 when Brezhnev ruled, we went to prison in 1981, we printed our papers in cellars for eight years. By 1988 the government could not feed the country without us. Gorbachev did not open the door; he only decided not to slam it on our fingers.

**Source C** — a report of the kind written by Western economists about Eastern Europe, 1988 (invented for this question)

> Industrial growth in the region has almost stopped. Poland and Hungary owe Western banks sums they cannot repay. Shortages of basic goods are worsening, and the Soviet Union, facing its own falling oil revenues and the costs of Afghanistan, can no longer afford to support its allies with cheap energy.

**Source D** — the diary of a fictional Leipzig nurse, 9 October 1989 (invented for this question)

> Seventy thousand of us walked round the ring road tonight with candles, shouting 'We are the people'. Everyone expected the soldiers to shoot, as in China in the summer. The trucks were there and the hospitals had been told to prepare blood. But nobody fired. Somebody said the Russians had refused to help.

**Source E** — a statement of the kind made by a Soviet foreign ministry spokesman to journalists, October 1989 (invented for this question)

> The Brezhnev Doctrine is dead. Every country decides for itself which road to take. We now have the 'Sinatra Doctrine': they do it their way.

**Source F** — an extract from a book by a fictional historian of the Cold War, 2009 (invented for this question)

> Gorbachev wanted to save socialism by reforming it, not to dismantle the Soviet bloc. His great decision was a negative one: not to use force. That decision was necessary for the peaceful revolutions of 1989, but it was not sufficient. The regimes fell because almost nobody was prepared to defend them.

**Background information.** In 1968 more than half a million American troops were in Vietnam. After the Tet Offensive of January 1968, President Johnson decided not to seek re-election. His successor, Richard Nixon, began to withdraw American troops in 1969, and the last American combat troops left after the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973.

Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a statement of the kind issued by the US military command in Saigon, March 1968 (invented for this question)

> The enemy's so-called general offensive has failed. He has lost tens of thousands of his best fighters and has not held a single city. The people of South Vietnam did not rise to support him. Our position is stronger than before.

**Source B** — a letter from a fictional American student to her college newspaper, May 1970 (invented for this question)

> Four students were shot dead at Kent State for protesting against the invasion of Cambodia. The President promised peace and widened the war. My brother's draft number comes up next month. We will strike, we will march, and we will not stop until every soldier comes home.

**Source C** — a cartoon of the kind published in American newspapers in 1971, described in words (described in words; invented for this question)

> A tired Uncle Sam, with a bandaged head, wades through a swamp labelled "Vietnam" carrying an enormous sack marked "Cost of the war". Ahead of him, a sign pointing backwards reads "Exit", but the mud reaches his chest.

**Source D** — the memoir of a fictional US Marine officer, published in 1985 (invented for this question)

> We won almost every fight and lost the war. The Viet Cong would melt into a village, we would call in the artillery, and the next week that village gave the enemy its sons. The Trail kept feeding them whatever we bombed. By 1969 my men knew they were there only until they could be brought home.

**Source E** — a speech of the kind made by a South Vietnamese politician to his parliament, 1972 (invented for this question)

> Our American friends tell us our army can now fight alone. Yet they are leaving because their own people are tired, not because the war is won. Our government must earn the trust of the villages, or no army will save it.

**Source F** — an extract from a book by a fictional American historian, 2005 (invented for this question)

> Withdrawal was driven by politics at home, but politics at home reflected realities in Vietnam: an enemy that could replace its losses, a South Vietnamese government that never won broad support, and a cost in lives and money that no President could justify for ever. Nixon also wanted to improve relations with China and the USSR, and an endless war stood in the way.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Mass production in the USA was pioneered by Henry Ford, who introduced the moving assembly line for the Model T in 1913. Each worker carried out one small task as the car moved past, cutting the time needed to build a car dramatically. Ford lowered his prices again and again, so that by the 1920s ordinary families could afford a car, and by the end of the decade millions of cars were on American roads. In 1927 Ford replaced the Model T with the Model A, as competition from General Motors grew.

The car industry stimulated many others. It used vast quantities of steel, rubber and glass, and created demand for petrol and oil. Governments built roads, and new businesses grew alongside them: garages, petrol stations, roadside restaurants and motels. Cars allowed people to live further from work, so suburbs spread, boosting the building industry.

At the same time more homes were connected to electricity, creating demand for new consumer goods such as radios, refrigerators, washing machines and vacuum cleaners. These were also mass-produced, and their prices fell.

Two developments helped people to buy. Hire purchase allowed families to pay a deposit and take the goods home, paying the rest in instalments, and banks lent freely. Advertising became a major industry, using magazines, billboards and the new radio stations to persuade Americans that they needed the latest products.

The Republican governments supported this growth with low taxes, especially Andrew Mellon's cuts for the rich, and with the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922, which protected American manufacturers from foreign competition.

By the late 1920s, however, the growth was slowing. Many families who could afford a car or a radio already had one, and factories were producing more than people could buy, which was one of the weaknesses that lay behind the Crash of 1929.

The Republican presidents Harding, Coolidge and Hoover believed in laissez-faire. They placed few regulations on business and did little to stop large companies from growing and dominating their industries. This gave businessmen the confidence to invest and expand. Andrew Mellon, Secretary of the Treasury, cut income taxes, especially for the rich, arguing that they would invest the money and create jobs; profits and share prices did rise strongly. The Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 protected American industry by making imported goods dearer, so Americans bought American goods. Judged by its contribution to business confidence and profits, government policy was clearly important.

However, if importance is judged by what actually created the new wealth, other factors matter more. The decisive factor was new technology and mass production. Ford's assembly line made cars cheap enough for ordinary families, and the car industry in turn boosted steel, rubber, glass, oil and road-building. Electrification created demand for radios, refrigerators and other consumer goods. Government policy did not invent any of this.

Demand also depended on credit, hire purchase and advertising, which let people buy goods before they had saved for them, and on rising confidence and share prices. The USA also began the decade with great advantages: it had gained markets and loans during the First World War, its territory had not been damaged, and it had vast natural resources.

Importance can also be judged by long-term effects. Here government policy looks important in a negative way. Laissez-faire meant that banks and the stock market were poorly regulated, tax cuts increased inequality, and tariffs led other countries to retaliate, hurting farmers and making it harder to export surplus goods. These policies contributed to the weaknesses that turned the Crash of 1929 into a depression.

Overall, government policy was important because it created conditions in which business could flourish and gave confidence to investors, but it was less important than mass production and new technology, which were the real engines of the boom. Its greatest importance may lie in its long-term contribution to the weaknesses of the economy.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Prohibition grew out of long campaigns by temperance groups such as the Anti-Saloon League and the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which blamed alcohol for crime, poverty and violence in the home. Many Protestant churches saw drinking as sinful, and the First World War added patriotic arguments, since grain was needed for food and many brewers were of German origin. The Eighteenth Amendment was ratified in 1919 and, enforced by the Volstead Act, Prohibition came into force in January 1920.

From the start, millions of Americans ignored it. Thousands of illegal bars, called speakeasies, opened in the cities. Bootleggers smuggled alcohol over the long borders with Canada and Mexico and by sea, and people made their own 'moonshine', which was sometimes poisonous.

Enforcement was weak. There were only a few thousand Prohibition agents for the whole country, and many police officers, judges and politicians were bribed to look the other way.

The huge profits from illegal alcohol fuelled organised crime. In Chicago, Al Capone controlled speakeasies, gambling and other rackets, and rival gangs fought violently for territory. On 14 February 1929, in the St Valentine's Day Massacre, seven men linked to a rival gang were shot dead in a Chicago garage. Capone was finally convicted in 1931, not for violence but for income-tax evasion.

By then many Americans believed Prohibition had failed: it had not stopped drinking, but it had increased crime and corruption and damaged respect for the law. The Depression after 1929 added economic arguments, since legal brewing would create jobs and the government could tax alcohol again. Franklin Roosevelt promised repeal in the 1932 election, and the Twenty-first Amendment ended Prohibition in December 1933.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The Ku Klux Klan was an important part of American society in the 1920s, but its importance depends on how it is judged.

Judged by its size, it was very important. Refounded in 1915, it grew rapidly in the early 1920s and spread far beyond the South, especially into the Midwest. Historians estimate that its membership reached several million in the mid-1920s, and in some states it had real political influence. This shows that its ideas of white Protestant supremacy were shared by a large number of ordinary Americans.

Judged by its impact on its victims, it was also important. The Klan targeted Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants, using intimidation, beatings and murder, and it spread fear in many communities. For the people it attacked, its importance cannot be measured simply in numbers.

However, other ways of judging importance suggest limits. The Klan's power was short-lived: after 1925, when one of its leaders in Indiana was convicted of a brutal murder, its hypocrisy was exposed and membership collapsed. Many Americans opposed or ridiculed it.

Moreover, much of the intolerance of the 1920s did not depend on the Klan. In the South, segregation was enforced by Jim Crow laws and most Black people were kept from voting by tests and taxes; lynching continued without a federal law to stop it. Nationally, Congress passed the immigration quotas of 1921 and 1924, and the Red Scare led to the Palmer Raids and the deportation of radicals. The Sacco and Vanzetti case and the Scopes trial show intolerance towards immigrants and modern ideas in the courts. These laws and events affected far more people for far longer than the Klan did.

The Klan is therefore most important as a symbol and a symptom: it shows how widespread nativist and racist attitudes were in the early 1920s. But as a cause of intolerance it was less important than the laws and institutions, such as segregation and immigration quotas, which outlasted its brief period of mass support.

Franklin D. Roosevelt became President on 4 March 1933, at the worst point of the Depression. About a quarter of the workforce was unemployed and the banking system was close to collapse. In his inaugural address he told Americans that the only thing they had to fear was fear itself, and he asked Congress for broad powers to deal with the emergency.

His first action was to declare a bank holiday, closing every bank. Congress quickly passed the Emergency Banking Act: government inspectors examined the banks, and only those judged sound reopened, with government support. In his first fireside chat on the radio Roosevelt explained the plan and urged people to trust the reopened banks, and when they reopened more money was deposited than withdrawn.

A flood of new laws followed. At the end of March the Civilian Conservation Corps was set up to give young unemployed men work planting trees and protecting the countryside, with most of their wages sent home. In May the Federal Emergency Relief Administration gave federal money to the states for relief. The Agricultural Adjustment Act paid farmers to produce less, so that prices would rise. The Tennessee Valley Authority was created to build dams in one of the poorest regions of the country, controlling floods and producing cheap electricity.

In June the National Industrial Recovery Act set up the National Recovery Administration, which encouraged employers to agree codes on fair prices, wages and hours, and the Public Works Administration, which funded roads, bridges, schools and dams. Other laws regulated the stock market and banks.

By mid-June, when the Hundred Days ended, Congress had passed a remarkable number of major laws, and Roosevelt had restored a sense that the government was acting to meet the crisis.

Opposition did limit the New Deal, but its importance varied, and other factors limited its achievements more.

The Supreme Court was the most direct obstacle. In May 1935 it struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act, ending the NRA codes, and in January 1936 it struck down the AAA. Roosevelt's plan to add up to six judges was defeated in Congress in 1937 and damaged his authority. Judged by its power to stop policies, the Court was very important.

Business and Republican opposition also mattered. The American Liberty League attacked the New Deal as a threat to freedom, and many business leaders, fearing regulation, taxes and stronger unions, held back investment, which slowed recovery. Southern Democrats in Congress shaped what the New Deal could do: Roosevelt avoided supporting a federal anti-lynching law to keep their votes, and farm and domestic workers, many of them Black, were at first left out of Social Security.

In other ways opposition failed or even pushed the New Deal further. Roosevelt won the 1936 election in a landslide, and after 1937 the Court accepted the Wagner Act and the Social Security Act. Critics on the left, such as Huey Long and Dr Townsend, encouraged Roosevelt to move towards reform, including Social Security and higher taxes on the rich. Judged by how far it changed the direction of policy, opposition from the left was arguably as important as opposition from the right.

Other factors limited the New Deal's achievements more. The Depression was enormous, and government spending, though large by earlier standards, was not enough to end mass unemployment. Roosevelt's own decision to cut spending in 1937 caused the recession of 1937-38. Many New Deal jobs were temporary, and the programmes themselves often treated Black Americans and women unequally.

Overall, opposition was important in restricting particular policies and in limiting the New Deal's reach to some groups, but the main limit on its achievements was the scale of the Depression and the caution of the New Deal itself, especially over spending.
